final_answer:
Short answer: under the Guidelines it should not matter which office indicts, so long as the chosen office can charge all of the false claims in a single indictment. Neither district gives the prosecutors a built-in guideline advantage. Caveat: I could not fetch any primary text (the egress proxy blocked ussc.gov, govinfo, Cornell, Justia and house.gov), so none of this is firewall-verified and I cite no authority as relied on. It rests on my recall of the rules and one search summary.

1. Guideline range is driven by conduct, not district. From memory, §2B1.1 sets the base offense level, with a loss table, and §2B1.1(b)(7) adds levels for federal health care offenses involving government health care programs with large losses. Relevant conduct under §1B1.3(a)(2) and grouping of fraud counts under §3D1.2(d) mean losses from both states' false claims would generally be aggregated in one range if they are part of the same course of conduct or common scheme. This is why a Georgia-only or South Carolina-only conviction should still carry the full-loss range. I did not verify the text.

2. No circuit-split advantage. The Eleventh Circuit (Georgia) en banc in United States v. Dupree (2023) held the commentary's 'intended loss' could not expand 'loss', while the Fourth Circuit (South Carolina) had not adopted that view. A search summary reports that the November 2024 amendment moved 'greater of actual or intended loss' into the guideline text itself, which would moot that difference. I did not verify the amendment text or the Fourth Circuit's position.

3. The real limit is the statutory maximum, so charging structure matters. §1347 carries up to 10 years per count (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death), as I recall. The guideline range can exceed 10 years only if enough counts are charged to permit stacking under §5G1.2(d). So the best office is the one that can bring the most counts covering all the fraud in one indictment. Venue under 18 U.S.C. §3237(a) lets an offense begun, continued or completed in more than one district be prosecuted in any of them. If the doctor ran one scheme across both states, either district may be able to charge the whole thing, and the office with the strongest venue link and most claims should do so. If the claims are two distinct executions, each district can charge only its own, so a single-district indictment would carry fewer counts and a lower statutory ceiling. In that case a joint approach, a prosecution in the district with the larger share of claims, or sequential prosecutions would need to be weighed. Sequential prosecutions risk less coordinated sentences and have double-jeopardy and consecutive-sentence questions I did not research.

Bottom line: either office, provided it has venue over the entire scheme and indicts all claims. If only one district's claims can be reached by each, then choose the district with the greater share of fraudulent claims and loss, or pursue a combined prosecution. The facts given do not show which district is larger.
